paragraphs: The count of the 248 words of the Shema is as follows: six of "Shema Yisrael," six of "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," forty-two of "Ve'ahavta," seventy-two of "Vehaya Im Shamoa" until "Vesamtem," fifty of "Vesamtem" until "Vayomer," and sixty-nine of "Vayomer" — that comes to a total of 245, and with the three words that the prayer leader (Shaliach Tzibbur) repeats, they are completed to 248. It is known that in this count of 248 there are profound intentions in every detail, and it is impossible for any single one of them to be missing for anyone. Therefore even an individual who recites the Shema — whether of Shacharit, whether of Arvit, or the Shema recited on the bed — must repeat the three words "Hashem Elokeichem Emet" in order to complete the 248. However, the prayer leader, by virtue of his role, has greater power in this completion by repeating those three words; therefore, if a person is praying with a congregation where a prayer leader is standing, he should hear the repetition from the prayer leader, and he himself need not repeat it, but should only have the intention of completing his own 248 through hearing the prayer leader's repetition. In my holy work "Makbetziel" I raised, with the help of Heaven, that if the one praying with the congregation is still in the middle of the Shema when the prayer leader has already finished the Shema and repeated the three mentioned words, it does not help him to complete it by that hearing, because the secret of the matter is that this repeated count must come last, at the conclusion of the Shema, and if he completes it in the middle, this mixes up the order, making the lower into the upper. Therefore in such a case it is better that he himself repeat the words and complete what is missing, and only if he finishes the Shema together with the prayer leader is it better to hear the repetition from the prayer leader.

clarification.explanation: The count of the 248 words of the Shema: 6 of "Shema Yisrael," 6 of "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto," 42 of "Ve'ahavta," 72 of "Vehaya Im Shamoa" until "Vesamtem," 50 from "Vesamtem" until "Vayomer," and 69 of "Vayomer" — that comes to 245, and with the three words that the prayer leader repeats they are completed to 248. In this count there are profound intentions in every detail, and it is impossible for a person to be missing any of it. Therefore even an individual reciting the Shema (Shacharit, Arvit, or on the bed) must repeat the three words "Hashem Elokeichem Emet" to complete the 248. But the prayer leader, by virtue of his role, has greater power in this completion; therefore one who prays with a congregation that has a prayer leader should hear the repetition from him and intend thereby to complete his own 248, and need not repeat it himself. Nevertheless (Makbetziel): if he is still in the middle of the Shema and the prayer leader has already finished and repeated the words — it will not help him to complete it by that hearing, since the secret of the matter is that the repetition must come last, at the end of the reading, and completing it in the middle would mix up the order; therefore in this case it is better that he repeat it himself. Only if he finishes the Shema together with the prayer leader is it better to hear the repetition from him.
takeaways: The Shema has 248 words — 245 in the reading itself plus 3 that the prayer leader repeats ("Hashem Elokeichem Emet"); an individual must repeat them himself to complete the count.

One praying with a congregation should hear the repetition from the prayer leader and intend to complete his count that way — but only if he finishes together with him, not if he is still in the middle.

paragraphs: Even though from the Torah the obligation of reciting the Shema is twice — once in Shacharit and once in Arvit — our Sages instituted four recitations of the Shema, all of them for the sake of the union (yichud) and pairing (zivug) accomplished above, in the aspect of the letters Vav-Heh of the Name. These four recitations of the Shema are not equal in their level. Their order of level, from lowest to highest, is as follows: the lowest of all is the Shema recited on the bed; above it is the Shema of Arvit; above that is the Shema of the sacrifices (Korbanot); and above that is the Shema of "Yotzer," which is the highest of all. And let a person not think that the Shema on the bed is only for protection from harmful forces; rather, it is an enactment of our Sages in order to draw down lights for the sake of the union and pairing accomplished above at the second midnight of the night, which continues and extends until the light of morning. The drawing down of these lights through this Shema will endure until the light of morning, and once the day is clearly established they depart, and they must be renewed again after morning. Since the first half of the day is very exalted, the union and pairing accomplished in it, in the Shacharit prayer, is also very great and exalted, and in accordance with its great worth it requires great preparation in the Shema. And although the Shema of "Yotzer" is itself very great, and the union accomplished through it is hidden and very exalted, nevertheless a person cannot achieve the complete rectification appropriate to the time of the Shacharit prayer through the Shema of "Yotzer" alone, because we do not have the capacity to draw down all the lights required for this time from all the levels at once — that is, in a single recitation of "Shema." Therefore our Sages instituted, before this Shema of "Yotzer," the Shema of the sacrifices, which we recite before the portion of the Tamid offering, so that we draw the lights down in stages: first we draw, through the Shema of the sacrifices, the light of one aspect, and afterward, through the Shema of "Yotzer," we draw an additional light of another aspect, which is a higher place than the first — and then, through this, the union and pairing is accomplished in the Shacharit prayer. Now the early pious ones, called the Vatikin, who were careful to recite the Shema of "Yotzer" before sunrise and finish it exactly at sunrise, did not need to recite the Shema of the sacrifices, because through the greatness and intensity of their piety they had great power in their intention and thought, and also because they recited it right before sunrise, which is very close to the departure of those lights of midnight — therefore they did not need to draw the higher lights required for Shacharit in stages as we need to, but it sufficed for them to draw the lights required for Shacharit in their single recitation. However, in the later generations, not every person is fit for this, and therefore now even the pious who pray the prayer of the Vatikin, reciting the Shema before sunrise, must recite the Shema twice — once of the sacrifices and once of "Yotzer." And that Shema of Arvit is for the sake of drawing the lights required for the union and pairing accomplished in the Arvit prayer. But for the sake of the union and pairing accomplished in the Minchah prayer, we do not need to recite the Shema, because the lights drawn in the Shema of Shacharit suffice for it — for even though they depart after the [morning] prayer, nevertheless, since the day is [the quality of] Chesed (kindness) and the judgments (dinim) do not dominate so much, they do not depart entirely, and a remainder of them stays behind, and this remainder suffices for the Minchah prayer alone. Therefore the union and pairing accomplished in the Shacharit prayer is far, far more exalted than that accomplished in the Minchah prayer, since what is accomplished in Minchah is from the remainder of the lights of the mind (mochin) of Shacharit, and therefore the judgments intensify in the Minchah prayer, since the lights of the mind go on diminishing. And the reason the Shema of Arvit does not suffice also for what is accomplished at midnight, when full judgments dominate, and therefore after the Arvit prayer the lights drawn through the Shema depart entirely, is why we need to recite the Shema on the bed, for the sake of the second midnight of the night. And as for why they advance the recitation of this Shema to the time of lying down and do not wait until the second midnight of the night arrives — this matter will be explained further on, in its place. And all that we have written here are the main points, what a simple person can bear in his understanding; but in truth these matters contain further profound secrets, which are explained at length in Sha'ar HaKavanot by our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation:
Although from the Torah the obligation to recite the Shema is twice a day (Shacharit and Arvit), the Sages instituted four recitations of the Shema, and all of them serve the union and pairing accomplished above (in the aspect of the letters Vav-Heh of the Name). These four recitations are not equal in level; their order from lowest to highest is: the Shema on the bed, the Shema of Arvit, the Shema of the sacrifices, and the Shema of "Yotzer" — the highest of all.

Let a person not think that the Shema on the bed exists only for protection from harmful forces; the Sages instituted it in order to draw lights for the sake of the union accomplished at the second midnight of the night, which continues and stands until the light of morning. Since the first half of the day is very exalted, the union accomplished in it in the Shacharit prayer is also very great and exalted, and it requires great preparation in the Shema. Although the Shema of "Yotzer" itself is great and exalted, we are not able to draw down all at once (in a single recitation) all the lights needed for this time from every level — therefore the Sages also instituted the Shema of the sacrifices (recited before the portion of the Tamid), which first draws down light of one aspect, and after it the Shema of "Yotzer" draws down a higher light — and only thus is the union needed for the Shacharit prayer completed. The ancient Vatikin, who recited the Shema of "Yotzer" right up against sunrise (very close to the departure of the lights of midnight), did not need the Shema of the sacrifices, because by the power of their holiness and intention they drew all the lights in a single recitation; but in the later generations we do not have such power, and therefore even those who pray as the Vatikin must recite the Shema twice — of the sacrifices and of "Yotzer."

The Shema of Arvit is intended for drawing the lights needed for the union accomplished in the Arvit prayer. By contrast, for the Minchah prayer there is no need for a separate Shema, because the remainder of the lights already drawn in the Shema of Shacharit suffices — since during the day (which is the quality of "chesed," and judgment does not dominate) the lights do not depart entirely after the prayer, and a remainder of them stays until Minchah. For this reason the union accomplished in Shacharit is far more exalted than that of Minchah, since in Minchah it is accomplished only from the remainder of the lights of Shacharit, and their power keeps diminishing. However, the Shema of Arvit itself is not sufficient for the sake of the union accomplished at midnight (when full judgment dominates), and therefore after Arvit these lights depart entirely — hence the need for the Shema on the bed, for the sake of the second midnight of the night. (Rabbi Yosef Chaim notes that all this is only the main points, as much as a simple person can bear in understanding, and that these matters contain further profound secrets explained at length in Sha'ar HaKavanot by our teacher the Ari.)
takeaways: The four recitations of the Shema (on the bed, Arvit, the sacrifices, Yotzer) are built in ascending levels, each one drawing light for a different higher union.

The Shema of the sacrifices was instituted because it is not possible to draw all the lights needed for Shacharit at once (in Yotzer alone) — so it is recited twice in sequence (sacrifices, then Yotzer), except for the ancient Vatikin of great holiness who managed with one.

The Shema of Minchah is unnecessary because the remaining light of Shacharit (a day of the quality of chesed) still remains; but the Shema of Arvit is not sufficient for midnight, so another Shema on the bed is required.

paragraphs: Its recitation should be before sunrise — that is, close to it, so that he finishes the Shema and its blessings exactly at sunrise, and joins the [Amidah] prayer immediately at sunrise. Whoever is able to do so has a great mitzvah in his hand and his reward is immense, even in this time when we do not have the strength of the early pious ones called the Vatikin. Nevertheless, if he did not recite it before sunrise, he should hasten to recite it as soon as possible, for the diligent act early with mitzvot. Now, as for the time of sunrise, Rav Beit David, of blessed memory, in Siman 36, page 11, established that it is one hour before the sun rises visibly to us over the land — see there. And in my responsum, with the help of Heaven, in my holy work Rav Pe'alim, I brought his words and wrote that his proofs are not conclusive, for there is room to respond. I also brought the words of Minchat Kohen and Ateret Rosh on Berachot page 6, from which it appears that they do not hold the opinion of Beit David, of blessed memory, based on the test of vision — for our Sages said that at midday the sun is over every person's head, and we observe that it is only after five and a half hours from the time the sun becomes visible to our eyes that the sun is over every person's head; but I wrote that this test only works in the summer months, not so in the winter months, and therefore there is no reliance on it. I wrote further that we have not found that the great later authorities brought the words of Rav Beit David, of blessed memory, to rely on them; we found only the Gaon Chida in Machazik Berachah, Siman 58, who noted and pointed to a place in the book Beit David mentioned, and also in his glosses on the Holy Zohar, part 2, page 196, he noted the words of the said Beit David, but did not reveal to us his agreement in the matter as halachah. And from his book Yosef Ometz, Siman 76, letter gimel, where he wrote, and these are his words: "Indeed I heard that something similar was practiced by the great and holy rabbi, our teacher Rabbi Yosef Kubo, regarding the morning prayer" — end of his words. And I deduced from this that in the time of the Gaon Chida, of blessed memory, they were not accustomed in the Holy City of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, and the Holy City of Hebron, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, to act according to the opinion of Rav Beit David, of blessed memory. Therefore, what we have heard, that now the custom of the pious of Beit El, may their Rock and Redeemer preserve them, in the Holy City of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, is to act according to the opinion of Rav Beit David in the Shema and prayer — this is a new custom that did not exist before. And the pious Rabbi, our teacher Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may the Merciful One preserve him, wrote that most of the congregation in Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and reestablished speedily, act as Rav Beit David, of blessed memory, wrote; nevertheless there are the meticulous who do not pray except after the sun has actually risen, as is written in the book Divrei Yosef, Schwartz, page 75, etc. Therefore I am accustomed to finish reciting the Shema six minutes — that is, a tenth of an hour — before the sun's actual appearance, and sometimes, due to the speed of the cantor, it will be ten or twelve minutes before the sun's appearance over the land, and I am not troubled by this; and likewise sometimes it will coincide with the sun's appearance, and I beseech God Almighty that He grant us merit to hit that exact point, for this requires the help of Heaven — end of his words, may the Merciful One preserve him. Now, here in our city, may it be built and established, the custom has recently spread to act, regarding the Shema and prayer, according to the opinion of Rav Beit David, of blessed memory. But certainly the custom of the meticulous is to pray with the sun's actual appearance as it becomes visible to us, and to begin the Shema six minutes before the sun's appearance — this is a correct and praiseworthy custom, according to my limited understanding.

clarification.explanation: The preferred time to recite the Shema is close to just before sunrise, so that one finishes the Shema and its blessings at sunrise and joins the [Amidah] prayer immediately at sunrise; whoever can do this has a great mitzvah and an immense reward, even in this era when we do not have the strength of the early pious ones (the Vatikin). Nevertheless, if one did not recite it before sunrise, he should hasten to recite it as soon as possible (for the diligent act early with mitzvot). Regarding the time of "sunrise," opinions differ: Rav Beit David wrote that it is one hour before the sun becomes visible to us over the land; the Ben Ish Chai (in Rav Pe'alim) disagreed that his proofs are not conclusive (and also that the test based on the sun's movement works only in summer, not winter), and that the great later authorities did not rely on him. It turns out that the custom of Beit El to pray according to Beit David is a new custom; and Rabbi Eliyahu Mani wrote that most of the congregation in Jerusalem follows Beit David, though there are meticulous people who pray only after the sun has actually risen — so he is accustomed to finish the Shema about six minutes before the sun's appearance. Recently the custom in our city has spread to follow Beit David; but in the Ben Ish Chai's own judgment, the custom of the meticulous — to pray with the sun's actual appearance, beginning the Shema about six minutes before — is the correct and praiseworthy one.
takeaways: Ideally one finishes reciting the Shema and its blessings at sunrise and joins the [Amidah] prayer immediately — a great mitzvah with an immense reward.

Opinions differ on the time of "sunrise": Beit David (one hour before the sun is visible) versus those who disagree; the Ben Ish Chai favors the custom of the meticulous — praying with the sun's actual appearance (beginning the Shema about six minutes before).

paragraphs: If one was under duress the whole night and did not recite the Shema of Arvit until the dawn (amud hashachar) rose, since the sun has not yet risen, he recites it and thereby partially fulfills his obligation of the Shema of Arvit, even though it will not benefit him regarding the rectifications accomplished above. However, he should not recite the Shema of Shacharit that day until after sunrise, for otherwise he would have two contradictory recitations.

clarification.explanation: One who was under duress the entire night and did not recite the Shema of Arvit until dawn rose — since the sun has not yet risen, he recites it and thereby partially fulfills his obligation of the Shema of Arvit (though it will not benefit the rectifications accomplished above). But he should not recite the Shema of Shacharit that same day except after sunrise, so that there will not be two contradictory recitations at the same time.
takeaways: One under duress who did not recite Arvit — recites it until sunrise and partially fulfills the obligation.
The Shema of Shacharit that day is recited only after sunrise.

paragraphs: The time for the Shema of Shacharit extends until a quarter of the day, in seasonal hours, and one must be careful in the winter months, when the day is short, that then the time for the Shema is short. Until one hour after a quarter of the day, one may still recite it with its blessings, but he does not have the reward of one who recites it in its proper time. And if an hour after a quarter of the day has passed, he should recite it without its blessings, like one reading in the Torah, on account of doubt regarding blessings, to be lenient.

clarification.explanation: The time for the Shema of Shacharit extends until a quarter of the day (in seasonal hours), and one must be careful in the winter months when the day is short and its time is short. Until one hour after a quarter of the day he can still recite it with its blessings, but he does not have the reward of one who recites it in its proper time. And if an hour after a quarter of the day has passed, he should recite it without its blessings, like one reading in the Torah, on account of the doubt regarding blessings, to be lenient.
takeaways: The time for the Shema is until a quarter of the day; until an hour after that — with blessings but without the full reward.
After that hour — without blessings.

paragraphs: Before reciting the Shema he should have the intention to fulfill the positive commandment that we were commanded to recite the Shema twice a day, as it is written, "and you shall speak of them... when you lie down and when you rise" (Deuteronomy 6:7). He should also intend to fulfill the positive commandment of unifying the Name, and he should close his eyes with his right hand during the first verse until he completes "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," and there is a secret in this matter. If he did not direct his heart to the plain meaning of the verse "Shema Yisrael," he has not fulfilled his obligation and must go back and repeat it. But if he became aware of this immediately after saying the verse "Shema," he should not go back to say the verse "Shema" a second time, for one who says "Shema, Shema" is silenced, so that he not appear to be acknowledging two authorities, God forbid; rather, he should be silent for the duration of reciting the first paragraph, and afterward go back and say the verse "Shema" and read from there onward in order. And if he wishes not to be silent but rather to finish the entire first paragraph and then go back and read a second time from the verse "Shema," indeed, he may do so as well, and this is preferable to silence. Also, regarding the verse "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" — some say that if he said it without proper intention, he goes back to say it with proper intention; however, when he goes back for the sake of "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," he goes back from the verse "Shema," so that the secret rectification of these verses will come in order.

clarification.explanation: Before the Shema he should intend to fulfill the positive commandment to recite the Shema twice a day, and to unify the Name. He should close his eyes with his right hand during the first verse until he completes "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed." If he did not direct his heart to the plain meaning of the words in the verse "Shema Yisrael," he has not fulfilled his obligation and must repeat it, but he should not say "Shema, Shema" (which would appear as acknowledging two authorities); rather he should pause, and then go back from the verse "Shema," or finish the whole paragraph and then repeat — and this is preferable. Likewise, if he did not say "Baruch Shem" with proper intention, some hold that he goes back to say it with intention, starting from the verse "Shema."
takeaways: He intends to fulfill the commandment and to unify the Name, and closes his eyes during the first verse.
If he erred in intention, he goes back from "Shema" — but never says "Shema" twice in immediate succession.

paragraphs: In the verse "Shema Yisrael," he should pause between each two words together, in order to direct his intention according to their single meaning. This is because "shema" means acceptance, as in "shamor veshamata" (Deuteronomy 12:28), which the Targum renders "tar utkabel" (keep and accept); it is also an expression of understanding, "shema" meaning "understand." And so here it says "Shema Yisrael," meaning: accept these words and understand them and know them, that you believe in them — namely, that Hashem is our God, and furthermore, that He is one Hashem. Thus in this there is acceptance and acknowledgment of two matters: the first is the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, in saying "Hashem Eloheinu," acknowledging that we have accepted His divinity, that He is a God to us and we are His servants; and the second is the matter of the unification of the Name, in saying "Hashem Echad," that He is without any other partnership, having no second, as Eliyahu, of blessed memory, said: "You are One, and not in number."

clarification.explanation: In the verse "Shema Yisrael" he should pause between each two words, to direct the intention. "Shema" means to accept and understand — accept these words and understand that Hashem is our God and that He is One. The verse contains two acknowledgments: the first is accepting the yoke of Heaven ("Hashem Eloheinu" — that we have accepted His divinity upon us), and the second is the unification of the Name ("Hashem Echad" — that He has no second and no other partnership with Him).
takeaways: Pause between the words of the first verse in order to direct the intention to its meaning.
The verse includes both accepting the yoke of Heaven (Hashem Eloheinu) and unifying the Name (Hashem Echad).

paragraphs: The letter Ayin of "Shema" and the letter Dalet of "Echad" are large letters. It is written in the manuscript book Keter Malchut that the reader must also mentally picture them as large letters, for the reader should visualize all the letters of the verse before his eyes in his mind, and these two letters he should picture as large — and this is correct.

clarification.explanation: The letter Ayin in the word "Shema" and the letter Dalet in the word "Echad" are written large. The reader should visualize in his mind all the letters of the verse before his eyes, and picture these two letters as large.
takeaways: One mentally pictures the letters of the verse, with the Ayin and the Dalet as large.

paragraphs: In the word "Echad," he should have in mind the combination of the Name Havayah with the Name Adnut, which is [pronounced] "Yah-ha-do-na-hai," and he should intend that they become equal in unity as one — this is the intention according to the plain meaning of the word "Echad." But he should lengthen the Dalet of "Echad," and at the time he lengthens it he should intend to give up his soul, [as if willing to accept] stoning, burning, execution by the sword, and strangulation, for the sanctification of the Name. He should also intend that through this acceptance his transgressions be atoned for, and that his nefesh, ruach, and neshamah rise up, as mayin nukvin (feminine waters), to the aspect of the letters Vav-Heh of the Name, and from there rise to the aspect of Yud-Heh, and from there to the aspect of the tip of the letter Yud, up to the very height of the levels. And if he has knowledge of the secret of Hashem and is able to broaden his intention, he should further intend that abundance be drawn from the Ein Sof (Infinite) to Atika Kadisha, and from Atika Kadisha to Abba and Imma, and from Abba and Imma to Zachar and Nekevah (male and female).

clarification.explanation: In the word "Echad," one should intend the combination of the Name Havayah with the Name Adnut, pronounced "Yah-ha-do-na-hai," intending that the two Names unite as one — this is the plain intention embedded in the word "Echad" itself. He should lengthen the letter Dalet of "Echad," and while lengthening it, give up his life in his mind for the sanctification of the Name (as though ready for stoning, burning, execution, and strangulation). He should intend that through this acceptance his transgressions be atoned for, and that his soul — the nefesh, ruach, and neshamah within him — rise as mayin nukvin, first to the aspect of Vav-Heh of the Name, and from there to the aspect of Yud-Heh of the Name, and from there further up to the tip of the letter Yud, the very height of the levels. And whoever has knowledge of the secret of Hashem and can broaden his intention should further intend that thereby abundance is drawn from the Ein Sof to Atika Kadisha, and from Atika Kadisha to Abba and Imma, and from Abba and Imma to Zachar and Nekevah.
takeaways: He lengthens the Dalet of "Echad" and gives up his life for the sanctification of the Name, while intending the union of Havayah and Adnut (Yah-ha-do-na-hai) as one.

He intends atonement for transgressions and the ascent of the soul through the levels of Vav-Heh, Yud-Heh, and the tip of the Yud; and one with deeper knowledge adds the intention of drawing abundance from the Ein Sof down to Zachar and Nekevah.

paragraphs: The word "Echad" is vocalized with a segol and a kamatz. Therefore he should say the Alef quickly, since the segol is a short vowel, and should not say the Chet quickly, since the kamatz is a long vowel. Also, apart from this, he must be careful not to lengthen the Alef, so that it should not appear as though he were saying "ei chad," meaning "there is no one," God forbid, as noted by the later authorities. And although we said above that he should lengthen the Dalet of "Echad," he must be careful not to snap the Dalet forcefully, so that it should not appear as though he were saying "da"; rather, he should lengthen it with a soft pronunciation, not a hard one.

clarification.explanation: The word "Echad" is vocalized with a segol (under the Alef) and a kamatz (under the Chet). Therefore he should say the Alef quickly (a short vowel) and not say the Chet quickly (a long vowel), and he should also not lengthen the Alef, so that it will not sound like "ei chad" (as if there were no One, God forbid). And although he lengthens the Dalet, he must be careful not to snap it forcefully (so that it sounds like "da"), but rather lengthen it with a soft, not hard, pronunciation.
takeaways: He says the Alef of "Echad" quickly and lengthens the Dalet, with a soft pronunciation.
He is careful that it not sound like "ei chad" nor like "da."

paragraphs: He should pause slightly between the verse "Shema" and the verse "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," and likewise he should pause slightly between the verse "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" and the verse "Ve'ahavta." And when he says the verse "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," he should bow his head slightly downward at the word "Malchuto," and there is a secret in this matter, to draw down illumination to the Shechinah, [called] Malchut, the mistress of the house. And although "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" is said in a whisper, nevertheless he should let it be heard somewhat to his own ears.

clarification.explanation: He should pause slightly between the verse "Shema" and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," and likewise between "Baruch Shem" and "Ve'ahavta." When he says "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto," he should bow his head slightly at the word "Malchuto," there being a secret in this, to draw down illumination to the Shechinah. And although he says "Baruch Shem" in a whisper, he should let it be heard somewhat to his own ears.
takeaways: He pauses slightly between the verses and bows his head at the word "Malchuto."
He says "Baruch Shem" in a whisper but still lets it be heard to his own ears.

paragraphs: One who recites the Shema must let what comes out of his mouth be heard by his own ears; but after the fact, if he did not let it be heard by his own ears, he has fulfilled his obligation. And those who are accustomed to say the verse "Hishamru" and the verse "Vechara" in a whisper must be careful to let them be heard by their own ears from the outset.

clarification.explanation: One who recites the Shema must let what comes from his mouth be heard by his own ears; after the fact, if he did not let it be heard, he has fulfilled his obligation. Those accustomed to saying the verse "Hishamru" and the verse "Vechara" in a whisper must be careful to let them be heard by their ears from the outset.
takeaways: One should let the words of the Shema be heard by his own ears (after the fact, he has fulfilled the obligation even without this).
Even verses said in a whisper should be let heard by his ear.

paragraphs: One who recites the Shema — whether of Shacharit, whether of Arvit, whether the Shema on the bed — should not gesture with his eyes, nor wink with his lips, nor make signs with his fingers during the first paragraph, even for the sake of a mitzvah. But from the second paragraph onward, it is permitted specifically for the sake of a mitzvah, and for something that is not for the sake of a mitzvah, it is forbidden. And one who gestures to a minor with his eyes or hands so that he pray is considered for the sake of a mitzvah, even though this minor is not yet obligated in prayer. And those charity collectors (gabba'im) who hold a collection box in their hand and go around the congregation collecting charity should not do so at the time the congregation is reciting the Shema, even though it is for the sake of a mitzvah, since, as he is walking about and collecting while still reciting, his recitation becomes a casual one. Likewise, here in our city, it is the custom of people to fan themselves with a small fan in the summer because of the heat; they must be warned not to fan themselves with their hand during the time of the Shema. And in Chesed LaAlafim, Siman 64, letter heh, it is written that one must be careful about sniffing tobacco powder and wiping the nose, even the second and third time, and even if he is silent during the sniffing and wiping, it is also forbidden — see there. But it seems to me that regarding wiping the nose, not all faces are alike, for sometimes mucus flows on its own, and if he does not hasten to wipe it, it will run down onto his lips and he will become repulsive to himself, and others will also find him repulsive because of him. And our Sages said, "Great is human dignity, which overrides a negative commandment," and especially where it causes others to become repulsed, which is very hard for them, particularly for a delicate person. Therefore it seems to me that in any such case, he should wipe it, even during the first paragraph, only remaining silent while he wipes.

clarification.explanation: One who recites the Shema should not gesture with his eyes, wink with his lips, or make signs with his fingers during the first paragraph, even for the sake of a mitzvah; from the second paragraph onward it is permitted for the sake of a mitzvah alone. Charity collectors should not collect during the Shema (since walking while collecting makes the recitation a casual one), and one fanning himself due to heat should be careful not to fan himself during the Shema. Likewise, one should not sniff tobacco. But regarding wiping the nose, when mucus runs down on its own and would make him and those around him repulsed, he should wipe it even during the first paragraph (remaining silent while wiping), for the sake of human dignity.
takeaways: One does not gesture with eyes or fingers during the first paragraph, and does not fan himself or collect charity [during the Shema].
Wiping a nose that has become repulsive is permitted even during the first paragraph, done in silence.

paragraphs: One who was walking along the road and wished to recite the Shema must stand still until [the word] "levavecha"; some say it suffices [to stand] for the first verse and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed." And one riding upon an animal should halt the animal for the first verse and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," but one sitting in a wagon need not stand still.

clarification.explanation: One walking along the road who wishes to recite the Shema must stand still until "levavecha" (some say it suffices for the first verse and "Baruch Shem"). One riding an animal should halt it for the first verse and "Baruch Shem," but one sitting in a wagon need not stand still.
takeaways: One walking stands still for the first verse; one riding halts the animal; one sitting in a wagon is exempt.

paragraphs: One who, while sitting, wishes to be stringent with himself and stand in order to recite the Shema standing, is called a transgressor if he does so for the sake of stringency; but if he does so in order to drive away sleep, it is permitted, as noted by the later authorities, of blessed memory.

clarification.explanation: One who is sitting and wishes to be stringent with himself by standing to recite the Shema while standing is called a transgressor if he does so for the sake of stringency. But if he stands in order to drive away sleep, it is permitted.
takeaways: One should not be stringent by standing for the Shema while sitting.
Standing in order to drive away sleep is permitted.

paragraphs: Although strictly speaking, if he was already standing anyway and wishes to recite the Shema standing, because it is comfortable for him to remain standing at that time, and he is not obligated to sit down in order to recite it sitting — nevertheless, according to the secret [teaching], sitting is preferable to standing, as I wrote in my holy work Makbetziel, from the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar HaKavanot, Derush 6, that one must now arouse the secret of the union above while we ourselves are below, in the World of Beriah (Creation), and therefore it is preferable to sit, since sitting indicates that we are still in the World of Beriah, for there is no [true] standing except in [the World of] Atzilut (Emanation), as noted there.

clarification.explanation: Although according to strict law, one who is already standing and finds it comfortable may recite the Shema standing, nevertheless according to the secret [teaching], sitting is preferable to standing. The reason is that one must arouse the secret of the union above while we are below in the World of Beriah, and sitting indicates that we are still in the World of Beriah (for true standing belongs only to the World of Atzilut), as mentioned there.
takeaways: According to the secret [teaching], it is preferable to recite the Shema seated.

paragraphs: If one is in doubt whether he recited the Shema or did not recite it, he must recite it, since the Shema is from the Torah, and a doubt regarding a matter of the Torah is resolved stringently. And even according to the opinion that says that only one verse or one paragraph is specifically from the Torah, he is nevertheless obligated, out of doubt, to recite all three paragraphs, since that was the enactment: whenever one recites the Torah-mandated Shema, he must recite all three paragraphs. Therefore, one who dozes off in the middle: if he knows for certain that he finished the first paragraph, he goes back from the second paragraph; if he does not know where he is, he goes back to the beginning. And if he stopped in the middle of the Shema due to an unavoidable circumstance — for instance, that the child relieved himself and he was forced to be silent — then, if he paused long enough to have finished the whole thing, that is, from the beginning of the Shema to its end, he must go back to the beginning; but if he stopped not due to an unavoidable circumstance but of his own will — that is, that had he wished, he could have continued reciting — then even if he paused for a long time, and even if he interrupted with speech, he need not go back to the beginning, but only to the place where he stopped.

clarification.explanation: One who is in doubt whether he recited the Shema must recite it, since the Shema is from the Torah and a doubt in a matter of the Torah is resolved stringently, and he recites all three paragraphs. One who dozes off in the middle: if he knows for certain he finished the first paragraph, he goes back from the second; if he does not know where he stopped, he goes back to the beginning. If he was interrupted due to an unavoidable circumstance (such as needing to be silent) and the pause lasted long enough to have finished the whole reading, he must go back to the beginning; but if he stopped voluntarily (that is, he could have continued had he wished), even if he paused a long time or spoke, he need only go back to where he stopped.
takeaways: In doubt whether he recited it — he recites all three paragraphs; in doubt where he stopped — he goes back to the beginning.
An interruption due to an unavoidable circumstance, lasting as long as the whole reading, requires going back to the beginning; a voluntary interruption requires returning only to where he stopped.

paragraphs: If one recited the Shema and then entered the synagogue and found the congregation reciting the Shema, he must recite the first verse and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" together with them; nevertheless, it is good that he recite the entire Shema with them, to the end, and receive the reward of one reading in the Torah. And if the congregation is reciting the Shema while he is standing in the [Pesukei De]zimra, after having said "Baruch SheAmar," then he should be silent while they recite the verse "Shema" and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," close his eyes, and think through the verse "Shema" and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" [in his mind]. But if he is standing in the Korbanot [section] or in the supplications, where he is permitted to interrupt, then he should interrupt and recite the first verse and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed" together with them.

clarification.explanation: One who already recited the Shema and entered the synagogue to find the congregation reciting the Shema must recite the first verse and "Baruch Shem" together with them (and it is good to recite the whole thing with them and receive the reward of one reading Torah). If he is standing in the Pesukei DeZimra (after "Baruch SheAmar") — he should be silent while they recite the verse and close his eyes and think it through in his mind; but if he is standing in Korbanot or in the supplications, where interruption is permitted, he interrupts and recites the first verse and "Baruch Shem" aloud with them.
takeaways: He recites the first verse with the congregation even though he already recited the Shema.
During Pesukei DeZimra he is silent and thinks it through; during Korbanot or supplications he interrupts and recites it aloud.

paragraphs: If he did not don tefillin and they became available to him after he had already begun "Yotzer," he puts them on between the sections (bein haperakim) and recites the blessing over them. These are the divisions between the sections: between the first blessing and the second blessing; between the second and "Shema"; between "Shema" and "Vehaya Im Shamoa"; between "Vehaya Im Shamoa" and "Vayomer." But between "Vayomer" and "Emet VeYatziv" he should not interrupt, for this is considered the middle of a section. All this applies to tefillin, since it is an obligation to recite the Shema while wearing tefillin, and therefore he recites the blessing over them. But if he did not don tzitzit and tzitzit became available to him, he puts them on between the sections without a blessing, and after the Amidah prayer he handles them and recites the blessing.

clarification.explanation: One who did not don tefillin, and they became available to him after he had already begun "Yotzer," puts them on between the sections and recites the blessing over them. The divisions between sections are: between the blessings, and between the second blessing and "Shema," and between the paragraphs; but between "Vayomer" and "Emet VeYatziv" he should not interrupt (as this is considered the middle of a section). This applies to tefillin, since there is an obligation to recite the Shema while wearing them, and therefore he recites the blessing. But tzitzit that became available to him — he puts them on between the sections without a blessing, and handles them and recites the blessing after the Amidah.
takeaways: Tefillin that become available — he puts them on between the sections and recites the blessing.
Tzitzit that become available — he puts them on without a blessing, and recites the blessing after the prayer.

paragraphs: For responding to Kaddish and Kedushah, and "Barechu," and "Modim," and the first five "Amens" of the Kaddish, he interrupts even in the middle of a section, and even in the middle of a verse; but when he interrupts in the middle of a verse and responds, he goes back afterward to the beginning of that verse, in any case. However, in the middle of the verse "Shema Yisrael," and likewise in the middle of the verse "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," and likewise between the verse "Shema" and the verse "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto Le'olam Va'ed," he should not interrupt at all, for anything of sanctity (kedushah). And if he was called up to the Torah while he is in the middle of reciting the Shema, he should not go up, even if he was called by his own name; however, if he is able to finish the entire Shema until he reaches the reader's platform (bimah), including saying "Emet VeYatziv, etc." until "this matter is upon us forever," and afterward recite the blessing over the Torah and read, he should do so.

clarification.explanation: To respond to Kaddish, Kedushah, "Barechu," "Modim," and the first five "Amens" of Kaddish, he interrupts even in the middle of a section and even in the middle of a verse, and when interrupting in the middle of a verse, he goes back afterward to the beginning of that verse. But in the middle of the verse "Shema Yisrael" and "Baruch Shem," and between the two verses, he should not interrupt at all for anything of sanctity. If he was called to the Torah while in the middle of the Shema, he should not go up, even if called by name — unless he can finish the entire Shema, including "Emet VeYatziv" until "this matter is upon us forever," by the time he reaches the platform, in which case he should do so and then recite the blessing over the Torah and read.
takeaways: He interrupts for matters of sanctity even in the middle of a section, but not during the first verse itself.
If called to the Torah in the middle of the Shema, he does not go up unless he can finish it by the time he reaches the platform.

paragraphs: When he reaches "and you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand," he handles the tefillin of the hand; at "and they shall be as frontlets," he handles the tefillin of the head; and he does likewise at the verse "and you shall bind them," as noted in the book of Kavanot. And although we wrote above, regarding the previous Sabbath, that Yotzer belongs to the World of Beriah and one should not kiss [the tefillin] except the tefillin of the hand, here it is different, for he is handling and kissing them out of love and cherishing of the mitzvah; therefore he handles both of them, since both are mentioned in the verse.

clarification.explanation: When he reaches "and you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand" he handles the tefillin of the hand, and at "and they shall be as frontlets" the tefillin of the head, and likewise at "and you shall bind them." Although in the blessings of the Shema (Yotzer) one kisses only the tefillin of the hand, here it is different — he handles and kisses both, out of love and cherishing of the mitzvah, since both are mentioned in the verse.
takeaways: He handles the tefillin of the hand and of the head when they are mentioned in the Shema.
He handles and kisses both, out of love for the mitzvah.

paragraphs: When he says "and you shall see it," he should look at the tzitzit in his hand twice, one after the other, and after each of these two times he should pass them over his eyes. And while looking at them he should intend that the numerical value of "ayin" (eye) is five, [corresponding to] the five appearances of the Name Havayah, and afterward kiss them. Likewise, when he says "and after your eyes," he should pass them over his eyes and kiss them, and there is a secret in this matter.

clarification.explanation: When he says "and you shall see it," he looks at the tzitzit in his hand twice, one after the other, and after each time passes them over his eyes. While looking at them he intends that the numerical value of "ayin" (eye) corresponds to the five appearances of the Name Havayah, and afterward kisses them. Likewise when he says "and after your eyes," he passes them over his eyes and kisses them, there being a secret in this.
takeaways: He looks at the tzitzit twice at "and you shall see it," passing them over his eyes and kissing them.
He does the same at "and after your eyes."
